newsitem.title: UK: BRIBE CASE SOCCER STAR APOLOGISES FOR LIES.
newsitem.headline: BRIBE CASE SOCCER STAR APOLOGISES FOR LIES.

text.p: Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers apologised on Wednesday for the "rubbish" he told police when being questioned about alleged match-rigging but said he made up lies to save his career.
"Everything in the interview is absolute rubbish and I apologise for that," Segers told a court in this southern England town.

Segers, 35, is accused along with former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, ex-Wimbledon and Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim of rigging soccer games for a Far Eastern gambling syndicate.

The prosecution case against Segers hangs on bank and telephone billing records, showing in particular a series of bunched calls around the dates of matches the player is alleged to have thrown matches or to have conducted money transactions.
All the defendants deny the charges, but Dutch-born Segers said he gave forecasts of Dutch games to Lim for his gambling friends in Indonesia, plus information about English teams.

He never took money to throw games in which he played, but he said English Football Association rules barred players from "assisting" gamblers and he was worried the information he had given would cost him his career.
In a panic, he told the police that money in an offshore account was the proceeds of juvenile car-thefts, and he denied knowing Lim.
But chief prosecutor David Calvert Smith said Segers had told "convoluted lies" because the money had come from throwing matches, and Lim was the middleman for the gambling syndicate.

He had even claimed to have been helped with the car thefts by a nephew who had since conveniently died. The nephew did exist and had died, but, as Segers now admitted, the thieving was a figment of his imagination.
"That's not panic, it's a brain working, isn't it, Mr Segers?" Calvert Smith said.

Segers said large cash deposits he made into a bank account came from three main sources -- his forecasting work, a business venture producing men's ties and from Fashanu at the start of a property business.

A Segers' defence witness, estate agent Imran Khan, provided evidence about the property venture, and the large amount of ready cash required as they were particularly interested in repossession deals that had to be closed quickly.

Segers also told the court he had summonsed his Dutch partner in the tie business to court, to explain why his slice of the profits were paid in cash to evade tax, and how much money the venture made, but the businessman had refused.

Calvert Smith asked him why the business partner brought "cash in a suitcase" over from Holland, as Segers had maintained, rather than simply transfer the money into his Swiss bank account from Spain or the Netherlands.
"In Spain we dealt with a lot of cash. In Spain they've got a bad reputation as bad payers," Segers said.

The prosecution alleges the tie venture never generated the large amounts of cash deposited, and Calvert Smith said it was quite unrealistic of Segers to suggest he got paid 1,500 pounds a week simply to forecast the outcome of Dutch games.
Calvert Smith pointed out that the money from Lim dried up after the Sun newspaper printed a story in November 1994 alleging that Grobbelaar had been taking money to throw games.
